I would like to invite authors of PRs to put the following self-declaration on their PRs if indeed true.

I, the author of this pull-request (PR) declare that: I have read and fully understand the changes being suggested in this PR; I have made sure that the documentation accurately represents the code and is written clearly and concisely; to the best of my ability I have checked that every new definition or lemma appears in the appropriate place within the project; and, going forward I will personally engage with the reviewer to make the code as good as possible and have done everything I can to minimize the effort the reviewer needs to put in.

If anyone has suggestions around this, I would be very glad to hear.
Sorry I missed this message, would this be a part of the PR description?

I was thinking of this, or we can find a generic message we can put to authors where we think is appropriate. For example:

Many thanks for this PR. Would you confirm that: you have read and fully understand the changes being suggested in this PR; you have made sure that the documentation accurately represents the code and is written clearly and concisely; to the best of your ability you have checked that every new definition or lemma appears in the appropriate place within the project; and, going forward you will personally engage with the reviewer to make the code as good as possible and have done everything you can to minimise the effort the reviewer needs to put in.

If not, please can you ensure this is the case before commenting -awaiting-author.

awaiting-author

How about something that an author writes in description/comment and then github bot takes off a specific tag?

By default we can assign: unconfirmed (or something similar) to a PR
and as soon as it detects "I confirm ..." it takes it off.
We can also then add this behaviour's description to the always-send bot message so that people know about it.

It will be then easy to filer PRs out for this specific reason.

Is the main advantage here us being able to filter out purely AI generated PRs?

effort required by reviewer<<effort put in by the author.\text{effort required by reviewer} << \text{effort put in by the author}.effort required by reviewer<<effort put in by the author.

What this means in practice is hard to quantify I think, but the work of making a good PR should not be put on the reviewer.

I think we actually solved this problem when we were discussing https://contributions.physlib.io/.

There are two types of activity that we often conflate in Physlib. These are “formalising” and “foundations”.

Formalising is the activity that most newcomers get involved in, corresponding to adding lemmas and definitions around areas which already exists. Here is where we have seen most of the surge in AI use.

Foundations is a different activity, it corresponds to setting down or improving the foundations in a given area. This often requires a lot of thought and discussion. The Standard Model project is an example of this.

I think foundations is what most of us who review enjoyed the most, but is where there are the fewest PRs.

I think we can do three things:

  1. Encourage people to work on foundations where possible and where they have the expertise.
  2. Introduce a “foundations” label which people can use to mark their PR as such. Theses will be prioritised.
  3. introduce a “blocked-by-Foundations” label which indicates that a formalisation has identified a inefficiency in the foundations of an area which should be addressed before the formalisation is merged.

what do people think?
This looks like the right direction to be going!
Would we also want to encourage authors of foundational work to start with writing API-maps and engage in discussions on zulip?

Will wait a bit to see if anyone objects :).

I wonder if we should instead of using e.g. feat(ClassicalMechanics):... be using e.g. form(ClassicalMechanics):... for a formalization and found(ClassicalMechanics): ... for foundations. This might be another way to do this

I am somewhat concerned that we just end up with a suboptimal corpus to the point where it is unfeasible to refactor completely, and the foundational work is left essentially disconnected from the wider material. Maybe AI will get good enough that any refactor can propagate through the rest and still be a net positive, but I think this is something to look out for (e.g. I don't think anyone seriously working on mathlib looks at Tau Ceti that much).
Could we prevent this by preventing further formalisation work in areas where the foundations need to be better thought through and adjusted?

I'm also a bit concerned about the API-map led design. Many formalisation quirks are exposed through the act of formalising, and what's a good API on paper may not directly translate to lean. It may still be a good idea to have a rough roadmap, but IMO the API-map and formalisation should inform each other and we should encourage discussion both ways.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Could we prevent this by preventing further formalisation work in areas where the foundations need to be better thought through and adjusted?

well I don't think that's really realistic, the pace of AI-assisted formalisation surely far exceeds that of foundations (I believe TauCeti is already larger than mathlib?)

I don't have a good solution to this, maybe we just need to be open minded and be willing to refactor stuff aggressively when needed.

Ok agreed. I think we should never be scared of refactoring, in fact I think it should be on of the core principles of the project. As you say, maybe the task of refactoring gets bigger as more stuff depends on an inefficient foundation; but hopefully we will find ways around this.

The above discussion is great and I largely agree with the points, but does it push us towards helping the root problem of reviewer effort or generally human effort? To me the foundations and formalizations is a mechanism which allows us to sort of slow things down and let the project develop in a more sustainable way. The number of PRs currently being opened is quite large and completely outpaces the number of reviewers available, if reviewers increase their pace, inevitably the reviewing standard will go down.

So counterintuitively, using being open to refactoring and letting formalizations that don't have settled foundations in at a rapid pace might (as mentioned above) make the process of refactoring intractable and lead to the below

Yeah I think the one thing we should avoid is reviewer standards going down - if that comes at the expense of review times then so be it. Most authors know how they can speed up the process, which is helping review. And ultimately we need more people willing to do this.

On the flip side, I think we currently have the philosophy (at least I do) that every pr can be made into something good and eventually merged. I don’t this is necessarily a good thing in the long run, and we (I) should get better at closing PRs where the work required outweighs the reward.

I’m also hoping that pushing people towards helping build better foundations will in the long run make reviewing formalisiations easier. IMO the easiest formalsiations to review are those in which the foundations are already set up in a good way.

For the record, I don’t think we should be letting in formalisations in areas where the foundations are currently not on at least a fairly solid footing. I think if we see formalsiations in this direction we should be encouraging people to work on the foundations. Maybe in PhyslibAlpha is ok, but there we can refactor very aggressively - deleting content if needed

So I consider us well setup to have the two-way design, the problem would be making sure people are appropriately using and modifying the API-maps as they add/change Lean content.

I have also been nervous about the balance of work on Physlib, and like Joseph said the foundations work is what I find most interesting and IMO a big goal of Physlib is to help solidify the mathematical foundations of physics and understand the "right" level of formality to think about different physical theories. But also on a more practical level I do worry that neglecting foundations is going to mean the different areas aren't going to be particularly compatible with each other.

I think there's a couple things contributing to the imbalance:

  1. Unfortunately foundations work is not that flashy and it is more exciting to work on big theorems. I feel like AI has made it a lot easier to target results you want without developing a lot of background.
  2. In some ways foundations is harder than advanced topics because while the theory involved in advanced topics is larger, the mathematical formalism is generally pretty clear. Foundations are talked about in many different ways that all need to be formalized and because they are the basics we usually neglect the details to make it easier to learn but that kind of stuff is important to formalization.

I agree that we probably don't want to shut down non-foundational work but maybe we do want to adjust the incentives because they aren't pointing in the best direction yet.

One thought I had was to put the foundational work (or anything we want to prioritize) into Github issues, and then we prioritize PRs that address/close Issues. Essentially saying, this is the priority for Physlib at the moment, you are more than welcome to submit other work but it may very well take some time to get to it. This would incentivize people who want to contribute to focus on project priorities without shutting down other work. The downside is more work to maintain the issues, but hopefully that would be offset work needed to refactor?

  1. Let the role of the GitHub issues be to signify to users that these are foundations that we want to see built, and that building foundations is important.
  2. However, use a foundations label to be the thing that actually signifies priority.

In this way, we don't need to make sure we cover every possible foundation task in the github issues for it to get priority.

I am probably on the extreme side of this but I presume everyone has certain areas of expertise and aren't equally qualified to review all domains.
